A confirmatory trial is powered for an effect in its whole population, and the
indication it supports describes a population in which efficacy and a
favourable benefit–risk balance have been concluded. Regulatory guidance asks
that this conclusion be examined across relevant subgroups rather than assumed,
and that a sub-population in which it does not hold be left out of the
indication; it credits a subgroup finding only when credible — tied to prior
plausibility and replication — and warns that an estimate singled out for its
extremity is biased by the selection (European Medicines Agency 2019).
Approvals have been restricted to a subgroup after a positive result in the
whole population (Amatya et al. 2021).

A subgroup of concern is reached by searching the trial's covariates after the
data are seen, or by examining many prespecified subgroups and singling one
out. Either way it is chosen for the extremity of its estimate, and its effect
is reported through the analysis the trial would have run had that subgroup
been the only one: the treatment coefficient of the trial's working model
fitted within it, a Cox log hazard ratio for a time-to-event outcome. So
chosen, the subgroup carries an estimate that overstates its effect, and the
same selection distorts the estimate for the patients outside it.
**forestsearch** is built for this situation. It does two things.

- **Identification.** It searches for a subgroup in the direction of a
  sub-optimal effect — the package's "harm" direction, a hazard ratio above one
  for a survival outcome. Every candidate is a conjunction of at most two
  covariate cuts, so whether a patient belongs is read from the patient's own
  measurements. Three identifiers share that form: forest search (León et al.
  2024), the causal forest of generalized random forests (GRF; Athey et al.
  2019, Cui et al. 2023) and the difference-in-natural-parameters estimator
  (DINA; Gao and Hastie 2025).
- **Inference after selection.** Refit-free multiplier resampling over the
  candidate family removes the optimism of selection from the estimate in the
  identified region and in its complement, and gives one-sided bounds on both
  (León and Anderson 2026a, 2026b).

**This vignette** runs the identification, by forest search, on the German
Breast Cancer Study Group (GBSG) trial that ships with **survival**, at the
settings of León and Anderson (2026b), and shows the call that adds the
inference. It takes a few seconds on one core.

The complete analysis — the three identifiers, the selection-adjusted bounds
for each identified region and its complement, and the declaration
calibration, which together are Table 1 of León and Anderson (2026b) run end
to end — is the article *Interpretable subgroup identification with
forestsearch*, listed under Articles on the
[package website](https://larry-leon.github.io/forestsearch/articles/).

## The data

The analysis set is the 686 patients with complete prognostic data, out of 720
randomized: 246 received hormonal therapy and 440 did not, with 299 recurrences
or deaths. Seven covariates enter the search: age, menopausal status, tumour
size, grade, the number of positive lymph nodes, and the progesterone and
estrogen receptor concentrations in fmol/l. Randomization status is masked in
the distributed data; hormonal therapy is analysed as randomized.

```{r data}
df <- survival::gbsg
df <- within(df, {
  id          <- seq_len(nrow(df))              # the fit's subject identifier
  time_months <- rfstime / 30.4375              # recurrence-free survival, days to months
  grade3      <- ifelse(grade == "3", 1, 0)     # grade 3 against grade 1 or 2
})
confounders <- c("age", "meno", "size", "grade3", "nodes", "pgr", "er")
stopifnot(nrow(df) == 686, sum(df$status) == 299)

whole <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hormon, data = df)
whole_hr <- c(est = unname(exp(coef(whole))), exp(confint(whole))[1, ])
c(patients = nrow(df), hormonal_therapy = sum(df$hormon == 1),
  none = sum(df$hormon == 0), events = sum(df$status))
sprintf("Whole-trial hazard ratio %.3f (%.3f, %.3f), hormonal therapy vs none",
        whole_hr[["est"]], whole_hr[[2]], whole_hr[[3]])
```

Every estimate below is read against the trial's own effect, a hazard ratio of
`r sprintf("%.3f", whole_hr[["est"]])`, and against clinically meaningful
effect sizes — not as a test at a hazard ratio of one.

## The specification

Candidates are conjunctions of at most two covariate cuts (`maxk = 2`) with
more than 60 patients (`n.min`) and ten events in each arm (`d0.min`,
`d1.min`). Continuous covariates take the package's default cuts, except that
the two receptors carry ten candidate cuts each (`conf.cont_jcuts`) with the
value zero — no measured receptor — forced in as a cut of its own
(`conf_force`).

Three thresholds govern the search, on the hazard-ratio scale with harm
upward:

- the **screening threshold** $c_1$ = `hr.threshold`, which a candidate's
  estimated hazard ratio must clear to be admitted;
- the **per-split threshold** $c_2$ = `hr.consistency`, the claim threshold
  at which an effect stops being beneficial, which both halves of a random
  half-split must clear for the split to count as consistent;
- the **consistency level** $p^\star$ = `pconsistency.threshold`, the
  proportion of consistent splits a candidate must reach.

León and Anderson (2026b) set $c_1 = c_2 = 1.0$ and $p^\star = 0.90$. The
splitting-consistency rate is *not* computed by drawing splits: with
`consistency_method = "resample"` (the default) it is evaluated in closed form
from one fit of the working model within the candidate, so nothing is drawn
and the search is deterministic given the data. The article gives the formula
and the fallback used when the closed form cannot be evaluated.

The **selection rule** is $\max_{\mathcal{A}} N(\varepsilon)$: among the
admitted candidates $\mathcal{A}$, the largest whose hazard ratio is within a
fraction $\varepsilon = 0.20$ of the largest hazard ratio over the family
(`sg_focus = "effMaxSG"`, `selection_rule = "neighborhood"`,
`effect_neighborhood = 0.20`). The rule is a modelling choice: it moves the
returned region along a frontier of size against effect, and so determines
what identification and inference are about.

## Forest search

One call. `parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential")` keeps the run on one
core; the package's default plan is parallel.

```{r fit-fs}
#| message: false
#| results: hide
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_fs <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  # the candidate family
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  # the identifier, its thresholds and the selection rule
  subgroup_method = "consistency", consistency_method = "resample",
  hr.threshold = 1.00, hr.consistency = 1.00, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
  stop_threshold = NULL,                      # evaluate every candidate; no early stop
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
fit_sec_fs <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

```{r fs-selected}
in_H <- fit_fs$df.est$treat.recommend[match(df$id, fit_fs$df.est$id)] == 0
stopifnot(!anyNA(in_H))
cat(sprintf("Identified subgroup: %s\n", paste(fit_fs$sg.harm, collapse = " & ")))
cat(sprintf("Patients in it: %d of %d. Fit: %.1f s\n", sum(in_H), nrow(df), fit_sec_fs))
```

The identified region is `r sprintf("\x60%s\x60", paste(fit_fs$sg.harm, collapse = " & "))`:
no measured estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor at most 26 fmol/l. One
argument in the call is not the default and is there for a reason:
`stop_threshold = NULL` has the consistency stage evaluate every screened
candidate rather than stop at the first that passes. Everything else that is
not the default is the specification itself.

### The search in numbers

The fit records how the candidates were whittled down.

```{r fs-funnel}
counts <- fit_fs$find.grps$filter_counts
funnel <- data.frame(
  stage = c("enumerated (at most two cuts, size-eligible)",
            "fittable (ten events in each arm, Cox fit obtained)",
            "clearing the screening threshold, HR > 1.0",
            "passing the consistency screen, p_cons >= 0.90"),
  candidates = c(counts$n_evaluated, counts$n_passed_cox, counts$n_passed_hr,
                 fit_fs$grp.consistency$n_passed))
knitr::kable(funnel, row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The candidates that pass the screen, with their size, hazard ratio and
consistency rate, are the points on which the selection rule acts.

```{r fs-candidates}
cand <- as.data.frame(fit_fs$grp.consistency$out_sg$result)
cand$candidate <- ifelse(cand$M.2 == "", cand$M.1, paste(cand$M.1, cand$M.2, sep = " & "))
cand <- cand[order(-cand$N), ]
knitr::kable(cand[, c("candidate", "N", "hr", "Pcons")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("candidate", "N", "HR", "p_cons"),
             caption = "The candidates passing the consistency screen, largest first.")
band <- (1 - 0.20) * max(cand$hr)
within_band <- cand$hr >= band
sel <- cand[within_band, ][which.max(cand$N[within_band]), ]
cat(sprintf("Largest HR over the family: %.2f (N %d). Band: HR >= %.2f.\n",
            max(cand$hr), cand$N[which.max(cand$hr)], band))
cat(sprintf("max N(eps) takes the largest candidate within the band: N %d, HR %.2f.\n",
            sel$N, sel$hr))
cat(sprintf("max N alone would take N %d (HR %.2f); max beta the N %d.\n",
            max(cand$N), cand$hr[which.max(cand$N)], cand$N[which.max(cand$hr)]))
stopifnot(sel$N == sum(in_H))   # the rule, re-applied, picks the fit's own selection
```

All of the passing candidates restrict the estrogen receptor, and the rules
differ only in how far that region is trimmed. The $\max_{\mathcal{A}}
N(\varepsilon)$ rule takes the 75 patients with no measured estrogen receptor
and progesterone receptor at most 26 fmol/l; $\max_{\mathcal{A}} N$ would take
the 82 with no measured estrogen receptor; the effect-maximising rules the 61
with, in addition, tumour size at most 35 mm.

## The region and its complement, before correction

The standard analysis within the identified region and within its complement:
the two-sample Cox fit of treatment, with its 95% Wald interval.

```{r unadjusted}
hr_ci <- function(d) {
  f <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hormon, data = d)
  ci <- exp(confint(f))
  sprintf("%.3f (%.3f, %.3f)", exp(coef(f)), ci[1, 1], ci[1, 2])
}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(set = c("identified region", "complement"),
             N = c(sum(in_H), sum(!in_H)),
             events = c(sum(df$status[in_H]), sum(df$status[!in_H])),
             unadjusted = c(hr_ci(df[in_H, ]), hr_ci(df[!in_H, ]))),
  col.names = c("", "N", "events", "unadjusted HR (95% CI)"), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "The identified region and its complement: unadjusted estimates, before any correction for the selection.")
```

These are not the estimates to report. The region was chosen for the
extremity of its estimate, so its hazard ratio overstates its effect, and the
same selection distorts the complement's. They are shown as what the
inference below corrects.

## Inference after selection

Adding `mr_inference = TRUE` to the same call has the fit correct both
estimates and bound them:

- **the correction** — refit-free multiplier resampling over the candidate
  family removes the optimism of selection from the estimate in the identified
  region $\hat H$ and in its complement $\hat H^{c}$ (León and Anderson 2026a);
- **one-sided bounds** — the *field* lower bound on the effect in $\hat H$,
  the *field-s* upper bound on the effect in $\hat H^{c}$, relevant to a
  benefit claim for the patients outside the subgroup, and the Bonferroni
  pair, which joins the two in one claim at a joint level (León and Anderson
  2026b).

The call is shown, not run, to keep this vignette short. The article runs it,
for all three identifiers, prints its fit times and reads the results.

```{r fit-fs-inference}
#| eval: false
fit_fs_inf <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  subgroup_method = "consistency", consistency_method = "resample",
  hr.threshold = 1.00, hr.consistency = 1.00, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
  stop_threshold = NULL,
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  # selection-adjusted inference
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", draws = 5000L, include_complement = TRUE,
                           field_scale_complement = "selected"),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
mr_estimates_table(fit_fs_inf, est.scale = "hr", digits = 3)
```

Each estimate and bound is read by its location against the trial's own effect
and against clinically meaningful effect sizes, not as a test at the null.
Whether and how to act on a finding is a broader judgement of benefit and
risk, which this inference is meant to inform.

## Where to go next

- The article *Interpretable subgroup identification with forestsearch*,
  listed under Articles on the
  [package website](https://larry-leon.github.io/forestsearch/articles/),
  continues this analysis: the selection-adjusted bounds for this region and
  its complement, the two model-based identifiers (DINA and GRF), Table 1 of
  León and Anderson (2026b), and the declaration calibration at a protected
  level.
- The [post-selection article](https://larry-leon.github.io/forestsearch/articles/survival-post-selection.html) reads the bounds in more depth on the
  same trial: the re-selection frequency p̂ as a diagnostic, membership
  agreement, and what each construction does and does not say.
- The [Guo and He article](https://larry-leon.github.io/forestsearch/articles/guohe-nested-continuum.html)
  sets the bounds beside the de-biased estimate and one-sided bound of Guo and
  He (2021) on a nested continuum of subgroups, Section S4 of León and
  Anderson (2026b).
- The ACTG 175 analyses are an article on the
  [package website](https://larry-leon.github.io/forestsearch/articles/):
  forest search on a binary and a continuous endpoint, with the bounds and
  the declaration calibration (León and Anderson 2026b, Section S3), and the
  three identifiers on the binary endpoint with the full bootstrap beside
  multiplier resampling (León and Anderson 2026a, Table S3).
- The package website carries the original workflow of León et al. (2024) —
  the full argument listing, the bootstrap bias correction and the
  cross-validation — as the article *Exploratory subgroup identification with
  forestsearch (the 2024 workflow)*, and the methodology and simulation
  articles.
- `?forestsearch` documents every argument, with examples on this trial and on
  the binary and continuous ACTG 175 endpoints, and a section on the options
  not tested against the manuscript analyses.
